about: The five notes of the ice-age maps (M3b, PR 2), written by hand in plain English from the notes research and its sceptic corrections (2 November 2026). Every sentence names the source ids that carry it; the ids are explained, with links, in data/sources.md (section 'Map data used in M3b: the age engine and notes'). Packed by tools/map/pack-age-notes.mjs into src/data/own/age-notes.json (links are not packed: the game page carries none). Heights are written 'now found N m up' (today's height of the old shore); dates we converted from radiocarbon years end with ', converted by us (IntCal20)' (checked again on 2 November 2026 with the IntCal20 curve, normal errors of 50 to 100 radiocarbon years assumed where the paper gives none); dates from bone and food-crust say 'may read too old (the reservoir effect)'; no 'BP'. marks: 'TO CHECK' (a fact or date not yet checked against a full source), 'not yet confirmed'. Narva wording and the neighbours inside the map were chosen by Ignas on 2 November 2026.

sentences.text: Ice still covers most of Finland, and its edge lies along the Salpausselkä ridges in southern Finland, laid down about 12,300 to 11,600 years ago.
In Sweden the ice still covers Stockholm and the land just south of it.
The Baltic is a huge freshwater lake held back by the ice, the Baltic Ice Lake, and its old shores are now found 140 to 160 m up in Finland.
In the far south the lake stood more than 20 m below today's sea, so parts of today's southern Baltic floor were dry land, where peat grew.
The land around Tallinn has lain under this lake since about 13,000 years ago.
In Lithuania the cold has thinned the forest to open land of juniper, dwarf birch, willow, herbs and grasses, and pine is slowly coming back.
Reindeer herds roam the eastern Baltic.

Small bands of reindeer hunters of the Swiderian tradition have come north from the south; one of their camps, Salaspils Laukskola near Riga, could date anywhere from about 10,500 to 9,000 BC, and how early people reached Lithuania is disputed.
In the south-west of the map, Ahrensburgian hunters camp on Rügen, Usedom, Wolin and Bornholm, then all joined by dry land, and hunt reindeer among other game.
On this map the water comes from the Swedish model (SGU), which leaves a strait between Bornholm and the mainland, so the map differs from that study there.
The last mammoths may still have lived in Estonia, near Puurmani.
The ice lake has just drained: around 9,650 BC its water poured out past Mount Billingen in Sweden, its level fell about 25 m, and the Yoldia Sea began.
The water stayed mostly fresh, with a short spell of slightly salty (brackish) water in the Gulf of Finland.
Most of today's Tallinn lies under water; only the highest parts of Nõmme, Lasnamäe and Viimsi stand out as islands, which grow as the land, freed of the ice's weight, slowly rises.
The map's water comes from the Swedish model (SGU), which is coarse outside Sweden, and it shows more of the Tallinn area dry than this study does.
The ice edge is drawing back north of the Salpausselkä ridges in Finland, and in Sweden it is near Stockholm.
Birch and pine woods spread over the thawing land, around openings of sedge and grass.
Reindeer are dying out in the region; the youngest dated bone is from about 9,800 to 9,300 BC, converted by us (IntCal20).
Late Swiderian hunters move through Latvia and Lithuania.
Estonia's first known camp, at Pulli, comes about 500 years later.
Around 8,750 BC the strait through central Sweden closed, and the Baltic became a rising freshwater lake, the Ancylus Lake.
At its peak, about 8,350 BC, its shore near Tallinn is now found 34 to 36 m up, and Toompea and Viimsi were islands.
The map's water comes from the Swedish model (SGU), which is coarse outside Sweden, and it shows the Tallinn area mostly dry.
Forests of pine and birch cover the land, and hazel has just reached north-west Estonia, about 8,700 to 8,300 BC, converted by us (IntCal20).
This is the early Kunda culture, which takes its name from a site in north Estonia.
At Pulli, on the Pärnu River a few km from the Baltic shore, people camped in spring and summer from about 9,000 to 8,550 BC.
The camp covered over 1,000 m², with five fireplaces and the sharpened ends of stakes, probably from huts; nine in ten of its mammal bones are elk and beaver, with fewer brown bear and wild boar.
Soon after, the river and then the rising lake buried the camp under several metres of sand.
Lake Ladoga is already a lake of its own, cut off from the Baltic after the Ancylus Lake's peak.

The sources disagree about the Baltic: the Swedish model (SGU) still shows a lake here, with the sea coming in only about 6,950 BC, while a study of the Tallinn shore dates a lasting link with the ocean, through the Danish straits, to about 7,850 to 7,550 BC.
Kunda culture hunters and fishers live across Estonia, Latvia and north-east Lithuania.
At Zvejnieki in north Latvia, on a ridge that was then an island in an old lake, a camp already stands, and the site later becomes one of the largest Stone Age cemeteries in northern Europe.
There, elk is the main game, with beaver and wild boar; bones of red deer and aurochs were used to make tools.

Its oldest graves are dated about 7,470 to 7,070 BC and 7,460 to 6,830 BC, converted by us (IntCal20), but dates from human bone may read too old (the reservoir effect, from eating fish), so the graves may be younger.
Ringed seals live in the Baltic; one of the earliest finds, from Kunda Lammasmägi, is from about 7,550 BC, converted by us (IntCal20).
The Baltic is now the brackish Litorina Sea.
Its highest shore was reached about 5,850 to 5,650 BC near Tallinn (the exact date there is not known; on Saaremaa it was about 5,850 to 5,750 BC), and that shore is now found 21 to 22 m up.
Broad-leaved trees are spreading towards their richest: elm and lime grow widely, and oak, a late arrival, spreads slowly.

In Estonia, people inland hunt elk, aurochs, red deer, roe deer, wild boar, beaver and wild horse and fish for pike, pikeperch and wels catfish; on the west Estonian islands they hunt ringed and grey seals.
The first pottery, made by people who still hunted and fished, appears (Narva-type pottery, about 5,200 to 3,900 BC); dates from food crusts on pots may read too old (the reservoir effect).
Burials go on at Zvejnieki.
To the south, in Kuyavia on the lower Vistula, farmers of the Linear Pottery culture have lived since about 5,300 BC; their time there ends about 5,050 to 5,000 BC.
